newsitem.title: INDIA: India, Bangladesh scheduled to sign water pact.
newsitem.headline: India, Bangladesh scheduled to sign water pact.

text.p: India and Bangladesh were set to sign a landmark treaty on Thursday to share Ganges River water, removing a longstanding irritant in relations between the two South Asian neighbours, officials said.

Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda and visiting Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina of Bangladesh were scheduled to sign the pact in the late morning on the last day of Hasina's three-day visit, officials said.
A senior Indian official said the treaty was expected to cover 25 years.
"It is going to be a long-term treaty but not to perpetuity," the official told Reuters in New Delhi.
The two sides clinched the outlines of the accord during talks late on Wednesday between Deve Gowda and Hasina, both of whom have been in power since June.
"I wish to place on record my profound satisfaction at the agreement we have just reached on the sharing of the Ganga waters," Deve Gowda said at a banquet on Wednesday evening.
"Without exaggeration we can say that we are opening a new chapter in Indo-Bangladesh relations (and) are also setting an example of cooperation and understanding," he said.

Deve Gowda was expected to announce the details of the treaty in parliament an hour after the signing ceremony, and the two leaders were scheduled to hold a joint news conference at 3 p.m. (0930 GMT).
The Times of India said the agreement called for increased dredging in Calcutta port, which like Bangladesh depends on water from the mighty Ganges.

"Let this agreement on the sharing of the Ganges waters be a stepping stone for greater cooperation between Bangladesh and India," Hasina said at the banquet. "We want to resolve this vexed issue once and for all."
Delegations from both sides met to hammer out the details after the two prime ministers held a half-hour private meeting on Wednesday, officials said.
The Ganges flows through northern India before emptying into the Bay of Bengal in Bangladesh.
Dhaka says India holds back water during the annual January-June dry season and releases excessive quantities during monsoon rains, causing flooding.
An agreement in 1977 to guarantee a minimum amount of water released from India was dropped five years later.
Hasina's Awami League party regained power in elections this year, 21 years after her father, independence leader Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, was assassinated in a bloody military coup.
Rahman became Bangladesh's first president after the Indian army fought a war with Pakistan which led to East Pakistan breaking away to become Bangladesh in 1971.
Hasina was accompanied by Foreign Minister Abdus Samad Azad and Water Resources Minister Abdur Razzak.

While water-sharing topped her agenda, Hasina was also expected to discuss the future of a 25-year-old friendship treaty her father signed in March 1972. The accord has been criticised as a compromise to India by Hasina's rivals.

Hasina's party said before elections this year there was no need to renew the 1972 accord because the seven-nation South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation, including both nations, served the same purpose.
